Paper explainer · arXiv 2610.31608 · ETH Zurich RSL

Humanoid Mobility via Attention-based Contacts

J. He, K. Wen, C. Zhang (equal contribution), C. Schwarke, Z. Zhang, K. Qu, S. Hu, M. Müller, V. Koltun, M. Hutter. ETH Zurich, NUS, Apple, ETH AI Center, NVIDIA. arxiv.org/abs/2610.31608

  • ProblemPure RL rarely discovers whole-body skills like a hand on a ledge. Motion tracking gives natural moves, but at run time it needs a full-body reference that fits the new terrain.
  • IdeaPredict only where 9 body parts should touch the terrain next (27 numbers). Let RL decide how the body gets there.
  • ResultOne policy on a Unitree G1 climbs ladders, crawls, vaults and gets up, with onboard LiDAR and no reference at run time. On 8 composite courses: 92.5% success vs 58.8% for the closest prior method (MGMT).
IdeaRun timeStage 1Stage 2Stage 3MappingResultsLimits
The idea

Contacts as the interface between seeing and moving

Earlier methods either give the controller nothing in between (pure RL) or a full-body trajectory (tracking). This paper puts a small, terrain-aligned plan in between: the next contact point for each of 9 body parts.

Contact plan, recomputed every step (50 Hz)
\[ \mathcal{C}_t=\big\{(\hat{\mathbf p}_b,\;\hat c_b)\big\}_{b=1}^{9},\qquad \hat{\mathbf p}_b\in\mathbb R^3,\quad \hat c_b\in[0,1] \]
\(\hat{\mathbf p}_b\): where body \(b\) makes its next contact within 1.5 s, in a gravity-aligned frame centred on the base and turned with its yaw. \(\hat c_b\): chance that a new contact happens at all. If \(\hat c_b \lt 0.5\), the target is set to \(\mathbf 0\).
At run time plannertracker

Two networks, both at 50 Hz

The tracker sees a small local scan, the contact plan and the goal. Most of its input is its own body state:

Action → joint targetspolicy 50 Hz · PD 200 Hz
\[ \mathbf q^{\text{target}}_t=\mathbf q_0+0.25\,\mathbf a_t,\qquad \mathbf a_t\in\mathbb R^{23} \]
Example: an action of \(0.4\) on the knee moves its target \(0.1\) rad away from the default pose \(\mathbf q_0\).
Stage 1 of 3 tracker only · RL

Learn to reach contacts taken from human motion

13.2 minutes of retargeted motion (box and ladder climbing, stairs, sitting, getting up, vaulting, stepping stones). The tracker gets the clip's contacts as input, not its joint angles.

Contact rewards in Stage 1 (weights 5.0 and 2.0)
\[ r_{\text{label}}=\frac19\sum_{b=1}^{9}c_b^{\text{meas}}\,\big(2c_b^{\text{ref}}-1\big) \qquad r_{\text{pos}}=\exp\!\Big(-\sum_{b}\big\lVert \mathbf p_b^{\text{exec}}-\mathbf p_b^{\text{ref}}\big\rVert^2/\sigma_c^2\Big) \]
\(r_{\text{label}}\): a body touching where the clip touches gives \(+\tfrac19\); touching where the clip has no contact gives \(-\tfrac19\); not touching gives 0. \(r_{\text{pos}}\): pulls each body toward the clip's contact point (\(\sigma_c=1\) m). Full-body terms (base pose, joints) remain in the reward too: the reference shapes the reward, but is not an input.

Check (paper Fig. 7A): contacts alone reach ≥ 98.5% success in every category. Adding 52 reference-kinematics inputs gave no consistent gain.

Stage 2 of 3 planner · supervisedtracker · RL

Learn to pick contacts from the map

The planner's main design choice is that it selects one of the 187 scanned terrain points (17×11) for each body. It does not regress x, y, z freely, so every target lies on a surface it has seen.

One query per body part (FiLM)d = 96
\[ \mathbf z=\mathrm{MLP}\big([\,\mathbf s_{t-4:t},\ \mathbf g,\ \textstyle\max_i \mathbf f_i\,]\big)\in\mathbb R^{96},\qquad [\gamma_b,\beta_b]=\mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf e_b),\qquad \mathbf q_b=\gamma_b\odot\mathbf z+\beta_b \]
One shared vector \(\mathbf z\) (body state, goal, pooled terrain feature) is scaled and shifted by a learned embedding \(\mathbf e_b\) of each body part. That yields 9 different questions, e.g. "where should the left hand go?"
Attention = affordance map over scan points32 heads in the paper; single-head form shown
\[ \alpha_{b,i}=\operatorname{softmax}_i\!\Big(\frac{\mathbf q_b^{\top}\mathbf k_i}{\sqrt d}\Big),\quad i=1,\dots,187 \] \[ \hat{\mathbf p}_b=\mathbf h_{i^\star},\qquad i^\star=\arg\max_i\alpha_{b,i}\qquad (k=1) \]
\(\mathbf h_i\): the 3-D position of scan point \(i\). The paper's decoder averages the top-\(k\) points with temperature-scaled weights; all reported numbers use \(k=1\), i.e. the single best point. Occupancy \(\hat c_b\) comes from a separate head on the attention output plus pooled terrain (96 + 64 inputs).

Training target: a soft 3-D blob, not one grid cell

Paper Eq. 1 · soft targetσa = 0.1 m
\[ p^{*}_{b,i}=\frac{\exp\!\big(-\lVert \mathbf h_i-\mathbf p_b^{*}\rVert_2^{2}/2\sigma_a^{2}\big)}{\sum_{j=1}^{187}\exp\!\big(-\lVert \mathbf h_j-\mathbf p_b^{*}\rVert_2^{2}/2\sigma_a^{2}\big)} \]
Distance is measured in 3-D, height included. On a ladder rung the nearest cell in x–y can be the floor below. The 3-D distance sends the weight to the cell that actually holds the rung. Try it:

Toy example: one 17-point row of the scan seen from the side (x, z only). Geometry is made up; only the formula is the paper's. Black dot = recorded hand position \(\mathbf p^*\), 6 cm in front of the rung's scan cell.

Paper Eq. 2 · planner loss
\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal L_{\text{planner}}={}&-\frac{\sum_{n}\sum_{b}c^{*}_{n,b}\sum_{i}p^{*}_{n,b,i}\log\alpha_{n,b,i}}{\max\!\big(1,\sum_n\sum_b c^{*}_{n,b}\big)}\\ &-\frac{1}{9N}\sum_{n}\sum_{b}\Big[c^{*}_{n,b}\log\hat c_{n,b}+(1-c^{*}_{n,b})\log(1-\hat c_{n,b})\Big] \end{aligned} \]
First term: cross-entropy between the soft target and the attention, counted only for bodies that really make a contact (\(c^*=1\)). Second term: binary cross-entropy for "will this body touch something in the next 1.5 s?", over all 9 bodies.

Where the labels come from: hindsight

Labels come from the tracker's own successful rollouts, not from the motion clips. So the planner only learns contacts the tracker can actually reach.

If no onset falls inside the window, \(c^*_b=0\). Episodes enter the buffer only if they succeed: a reference run that starts in the first 10% of the clip and reaches 90% of it, or a goal run that gets within 0.5 m (horizontal) and 0.1 m (vertical) of the goal.

Handing control from the reference to the planner

Supplementary Eq. · two linear schedulesu = PPO iteration
\[ \eta_{\xi}(u)=\begin{cases}0, & u\le u_{\xi}\\[2pt] \dfrac{u-u_{\xi}}{N_{\text{ann}}}, & u_{\xi}\lt u\lt u_{\xi}+N_{\text{ann}}\\[4pt] 1, & u\ge u_{\xi}+N_{\text{ann}}\end{cases}\qquad \xi\in\{\text{obs},\text{rew}\},\quad u_{\text{rew}}\gt u_{\text{obs}} \]
\(\eta_{\text{obs}}\): chance that, at a given step, the tracker sees planner contacts instead of reference contacts (the whole command is swapped, never blended). \(\eta_{\text{rew}}\): moves reward weight from the reference contacts \(5.0,\,2.0,\,1.0\to\times(1-\eta_{\text{rew}})\) to the planner contacts \(1.5\,\eta_{\text{rew}}\).
Stage 3 of 3 planner + tracker · bootstrapping

Go beyond the motion data with RL

New procedural terrains with no reference motion: ladders at 50–65°, vaults, gaps, beams, pallets, stones, rough ground. The planner proposes contacts, the tracker tries them, and successful runs become new planner labels.

Follow the planner (weight 1.5)
\[ r_{\text{plan}}=\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\sum_b m_b\,\lVert \mathbf p_b^{\text{exec}}-\hat{\mathbf p}_b\rVert^2}{\sigma_c^{2}\,\max\!\big(1,\sum_b m_b\big)}\Big) \]
\(m_b\) = 1 if body \(b\) has an active planner target (\(\hat c_b \ge 0.5\)). Average squared miss over active bodies.
Reach the goal (weights 40 and 20)
\[ r_{\text{move}}=(1-g_{xy})\,g_v+g_{xy}\,g_z \qquad r_{\text{stand}}=g_{xy}\,g_h\,g_\psi\,\exp\!\big(-(d_{\text{foot}}+d_{\text{tilt}}+d_q)/3\big) \]
All \(g\) are 0/1 switches. \(g_{xy}\): within 0.5 m of the goal. \(g_v\): moving toward it faster than 0.1 m/s without exceeding the speed cap (0.8 m/s on stairs, 2.0 m/s elsewhere). \(g_h, g_\psi\): height within 0.2 m and heading within 0.5 rad. Example: 2 m away, walking at 0.5 m/s toward the goal → \(r_{\text{move}}=1\). Standing still 2 m away → 0.
  • Two critics. \(V_m\) values reference-following, \(V_{\text{fs}}\) values goal-reaching. Advantages are normalised separately because the reward scales differ.
  • Buffer quality. Goal-reaching runs are kept per terrain tile; runs with less positive mechanical work per metre of goal distance are kept first.
  • Planner updates. 10 Adam steps per PPO iteration, 4,096 buffer samples each.

What training cost

Perception

Seeing ladder rungs with a head-mounted LiDAR

Sparse LiDAR hits are put into a 3 cm grid. A small CNN then decides, cell by cell, what to do with each height.

Per-cell mode choicegrid [−3, 3] × [−1.5, 1.5] m
\[ m^\star=\arg\max_{m}\ \ell_m,\qquad \hat z=\begin{cases} z_{\text{measured}} & m^\star=\text{keep}\\ \text{mean of neighbours} & m^\star=\text{average}\\ \text{empty} & m^\star=\text{drop}\end{cases} \]
Disagreement between the three mode probabilities serves as the uncertainty. Choosing a mode instead of predicting a dense map lets one network handle any scan sparsity. Trained with cross-entropy on noisy synthetic scans.

Overhang rule: if a cell already holds a confident height (uncertainty < 0.15 m), a new point more than 0.15 m below it is dropped unless its elevation angle is above −40°. This keeps a rung seen from afar from being erased by the floor seen up close. Runs in 30 ms per 10 Hz scan (20,000 points) on the Jetson Orin NX CPU.

Results

What it achieves

92.5%success on 8 composite courses (MGMT: 58.8%)
+54.8 ppStage 3 gain on sparse whole-body terrain (ladders, vaults)
≥ 98.5%Stage 1 success with contacts as the only reference input
11 / 11terrain categories where it beats MGMT
Limits (from the paper)

What it can't do yet

  • 2.5-D only. The map is a height field, so no overhead grabs, hanging or manipulation.
  • Local goals only. Waypoints are given by hand; there is no global navigation.
  • Same contacts, different motion. A backflip and a vertical jump have the same contact sequence, so the contact plan cannot tell them apart.
